## What each scenario is

- **Static page** — GET / — an 11.6 KB prerendered page, 200 + ETag
- **Revalidation (304)** — GET / with If-None-Match = that ETag
- **SSR, data unchanged** — GET /todos/t3 — rendered from path params + loaded data
- **SSR, data changes every request** — GET /live — nothing may be answered from memory

## Versions

- shinkansen (this commit) — this repo
- node:http v26.7.0 — raw Node, no framework
- Fastify 5.12.5
- Hono 4.13.8
- Express 5.2.1
- Next.js 16.3.6
- Nuxt 4.5.2

## Reading it honestly

- Already-answered URLs come from a table of pre-encoded bytes: the ETag is the CID of those bytes, so the answer is a value. That is where the static and 304 numbers come from.
- When the data changes on every request, shinkansen costs 8.0× the CPU of plain node:http: the app's render and the CID encoding run interpreted (kbb/sci), the others run V8-JIT'd JavaScript. Next.js costs 2.1× of shinkansen there.
- Compiling that render instead (.kotoba, amu --target js) is not a way out yet: after kotoba-lang/kotoba-script#103 (fixed; it was ~50× slower) it measures ~3–6× the interpreted .cljc, the rest being per-call type checks (#104). See bench/README.md.
- Next.js and Nuxt serve the same bytes through Route Handlers and Nitro server routes, each with its best documented static option. Next.js's force-static route ignores If-None-Match, so its 304 runs on a dynamic handler.
- The machine was shared (1-minute load average 136 when the run finished). CPU per response holds up under that; requests per second does not.

Method, fixtures and how to re-run: [bench/README.md](https://github.com/kotoba-lang/shinkansen/blob/main/bench/README.md). Raw medians: [bench/results/2026-09-23-c.edn](https://github.com/kotoba-lang/shinkansen/blob/main/bench/results/2026-09-23-c.edn).
